debugging.notes: Full traceback reading (deferred by B01) is read_tracebacks; f"{x=}" (deferred by B03) is in print_debugging. The editor debugger (deferred by B01 ide_editor) is use_a_debugger, non-core because it needs an editor with a debugger. KeyError and FileNotFoundError are not in common_error_types: dicts (B07) and files (B10) run in parallel and should show their own errors. Hand-tracing with trace tables is practised inside systematic_process rather than given its own topic. Rubber-duck debugging and logging (the logging module) were not given topics.

exceptions.notes: try/except on bad input (deferred by B02/B04) starts in try_except_basics; the re-ask loop is defensive_programming.get_int_helper. try/except around open() and FileNotFoundError belong to B10 file_io, and finally-for-closing-files / with to B10 context_managers, which should encompass exceptions.else_and_finally. KeyError handling and dict.get as the alternative belong to B07 dictionaries. Exceptions in Selenium/Tkinter projects are left to those library batches. Exception hierarchy is touched only via LookupError in several_handlers_and_as KP4.

raising_exceptions.notes: Re-raising with a bare raise is exceptions.propagation KP4. custom_exceptions teaches 'class X(Exception): pass' as a template and has pending concept:classes; the OOP batch (inheritance) should encompass it and may add exception attributes / __init__. Raising in constructors (validating attributes) belongs to the OOP batch (constructors). raise ... from e (exception chaining) was not given a topic.

defensive_programming.notes: Concept is titled 'Input validation'. Range-only re-prompting is B04 while_loops.input_validation; this batch adds non-numeric input. Validating with regular expressions (cs50p Week 7) belongs to the regular_expressions batch, which should encompass clean_and_validate_text. Preconditions as specs are B05 docstrings.specifications; raising on bad arguments is raising_exceptions.raise_builtin.

assertions.notes: Only one topic: using assert to write tests is owned by unit_testing (test_function_with_asserts), since assertions 'is part of' unit_testing.

unit_testing.notes: Depends on functions.main_and_helpers as B05 suggested, not on main_guard (which waits for B13). Core topics keep tests in the same file as the code, so no import is needed; test files that import the code are lib_pytest (pending concept:modules_imports). Doctests (deferred by B05 docstrings) are unit_testing.doctests, non-core and taught by no course. unittest_module needs class syntax (pending concept:classes). Test fixtures, skipping, mocking and parametrised tests were not given topics (codecademy only); testing printed output (capsys) also left out.

lib_pytest.notes: Non-core: needs a terminal and an installed package. 'pip install pytest' is shown as a memorised line; installing packages is tool_pip / third_party_packages in a later batch, which could become a prerequisite. 'with pytest.raises' uses with before B10 context_managers, as a memorised form. @pytest.mark.parametrize needs decorators (B08) and was left out; a later stitching pass could add it. Reconciliation: write_and_run_tests now depends on modules_imports.own_modules and tool_pip.pip_install; raises_and_test_folders on modules_imports.packages_and_import_errors.

tool_mypy.notes: One non-core topic (cs50p introduces it only). Uses list[str] in one example; container hints are B06/B07. Strict mode and mypy configuration were left out.

topics.title: Reading a traceback
topics.summary: Read a full traceback bottom-up: the error type and message, the failing line, and the chain of calls that led there.

knowledge_points.title: Read the last line first: error type and message
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(10 / 0)
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
The last line names the kind of error (before the colon) and what went wrong (after it).
knowledge_points.practice: Given short tracebacks, name the error type and say in words what went wrong.

knowledge_points.title: Tracebacks through function calls: the bottom frame is where it broke
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def average(total, count):
    return total / count

def report(total, count):
    print(average(total, count))

report(10, 0)
# Traceback lists: line 7 in <module>, line 5 in report, line 2 in average
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
"Most recent call last": read up from the bottom to see who called whom.
knowledge_points.practice: For a three-frame traceback, give the line that raised the error and the order of calls that led there.

knowledge_points.title: The line that fails is not always the line that is wrong
knowledge_points.worked_example:
In the traceback above, line 2 divides correctly; the bad value 0 came from report(10, 0) on line 7.
Follow the frames upward until you reach the line that supplied the bad value.
knowledge_points.practice: Given a traceback and the code, pick the line that should be changed to fix the bug.

knowledge_points.title: Use the hints: 'Did you mean' and the ^^^ markers
knowledge_points.worked_example:
total = 5
print(totl)
# NameError: name 'totl' is not defined. Did you mean: 'total'?
In Python 3.11+ ~~~ and ^^^ under the code point at the exact part of the line that failed.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix snippets using only the information in the error message, then predict the message for a new typo.

topics.title: Recognising the common error types
topics.summary: Match SyntaxError, IndentationError, NameError, TypeError, ValueError, IndexError, ZeroDivisionError and AttributeError to the kinds of mistake that cause them.

knowledge_points.title: SyntaxError and IndentationError: the code is not valid Python
knowledge_points.worked_example:
if True:
print("x")
# IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'if' statement on line 1
These are found before any line runs, so nothing is printed.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which snippets fail before running and fix the missing colon, bracket, quote or indent.

knowledge_points.title: NameError: a misspelled or not-yet-assigned name
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(score)
score = 10
# NameError: name 'score' is not defined
Names must be assigned before the line that uses them, spelled exactly the same.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether each snippet prints or raises NameError; fix the typo or the order.

knowledge_points.title: TypeError vs ValueError: wrong kind of value vs bad value of the right kind
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Age: " + 30)   # TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
int("ten")            # ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'ten'
int() accepts strings, so "ten" is the right type with a bad value.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify each failing line as TypeError or ValueError, designed so that both are plausible.

knowledge_points.title: IndexError, ZeroDivisionError and AttributeError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(nums[3])        # IndexError: list index out of range
name = "ada"
name.push("x")        # AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'push'
knowledge_points.practice: Match eight snippets to the error each raises; fix two of them.

topics.title: Finding logic errors with print
topics.summary: Spot a logic error (the program runs but gives the wrong answer) and locate it by printing values at checkpoints, including inside a loop.

knowledge_points.title: Logic errors: no message, just a wrong answer
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    for i in range(1, n):
        total += i
    return total

print(sum_to(3))   # 3, but 1 + 2 + 3 is 6
No traceback appears, so you must compare the output to what you expected.
knowledge_points.practice: For each snippet, say whether it has a syntax error, a runtime error or a logic error, and give the expected vs actual output.

knowledge_points.title: Print checkpoints to see what values really are
knowledge_points.worked_example:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 3):
    print("adding", i)
    total += i
The printed values 1, 2 show that 3 is never added: range stops before its end.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose where to put one print to tell two suspected causes apart; predict what it shows.

knowledge_points.title: f"{x=}" prints a name and its value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 4
print(f"{x=}")            # x=4
total = 0
for n in range(1, 4):
    total += n
    print(f"{n=} {total=}")  # n=1 total=1 / n=2 total=3 / n=3 total=6
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the debug lines printed by a loop; write a one-line debug print for given names.

knowledge_points.title: Find the first pass that goes wrong, fix it, then remove the prints
knowledge_points.worked_example: Print the loop variable and the accumulator each pass, compare with a hand-worked table, and stop at the first row that differs; that pass contains the bug.
knowledge_points.practice: Given debug output and the expected values, give the first wrong pass and fix the line responsible.

topics.title: Debugging step by step: reproduce, shrink, trace, fix
topics.summary: Work through a bug methodically: state expected vs actual, find the smallest failing input, hand-trace to the first difference, change one thing and re-check.

knowledge_points.title: Reproduce: write down the input, the expected and the actual result
knowledge_points.practice: From a bug report, pick the input/expected/actual triple that reproduces it.

knowledge_points.title: Shrink the failing input
knowledge_points.worked_example: largest([-5, -2, -9]) fails; so does largest([-5]). The one-item case shows the bug is in the starting value, not in the comparison.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the smallest input that still shows a given bug; explain what it rules out.

knowledge_points.title: Hand-trace with a table until expected and actual differ
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n  | best (actual) | best (expected)
start | 0       | -5
The very first row differs: best should start at nums[0], not 0.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in a trace table for a buggy function and mark the first row where it goes wrong.

knowledge_points.title: Change one thing, then re-run every case you have
knowledge_points.worked_example: Fix: best = nums[0]. Re-run [3, 8, 1] and [-5, -2, -9]: 8 and -2. Changing several lines at once makes it impossible to tell which change mattered.
knowledge_points.practice: Given a list of candidate edits, choose the single minimal fix and predict the outputs of all earlier cases after it.

topics.title: Stepping through code with a debugger
topics.summary: Pause a program at a breakpoint, inspect variables, and step over or into lines to watch it run.

knowledge_points.title: Set a breakpoint and run in debug mode
knowledge_points.worked_example:
1. Click left of line 4 to set a breakpoint (a red dot).
2. Start debugging (F5 in VS Code).
The program pauses before line 4 runs, so variables show values from lines 1-3.
knowledge_points.practice: Given code and a breakpoint line, choose which variables exist and their values at the pause.

knowledge_points.title: Step over: run one line and pause again
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Paused at total += i with i=1, total=0; Step Over -> i=1, total=1; Step Over -> back at for, then i=2.
The Variables panel replaces a page of debug prints.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the Variables panel after each of four Step Over clicks.

knowledge_points.title: Step into a function call; step out to return
knowledge_points.worked_example: Paused at print(average(10, 4)): Step Into jumps to the first line of average; Step Out finishes it and returns to the caller with the result.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which line is highlighted after a sequence of Step Over / Into / Out commands.

knowledge_points.title: Continue to the next breakpoint, or pause from code with breakpoint()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Continue runs until the next breakpoint (e.g. the next pass of a loop).
Writing breakpoint() on a line pauses there in Python's built-in debugger (pdb) even without an editor.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the fastest command sequence to reach the 5th pass of a loop.

topics.title: Catching an error with try and except
topics.summary: Wrap a risky line in try/except ValueError so bad input is handled instead of crashing the program, and know which lines run.

knowledge_points.title: try/except keeps the program running
knowledge_points.worked_example:
text = input("Age: ")
try:
    age = int(text)
    print("Next year:", age + 1)
except ValueError:
    print("Please type a whole number")
print("Bye")
# typing ten -> Please type a whole number / Bye
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output for several typed answers (digits, words, decimals).

knowledge_points.title: When the error happens, the rest of try is skipped
knowledge_points.worked_example:
text = "abc"
try:
    n = int(text)
    print("converted")
except ValueError:
    print("not a number")
print("done")
# not a number
# done
knowledge_points.practice: Trace which lines run for a good and a bad value; reorder lines of a try/except (Parsons).

knowledge_points.title: except only catches the error type it names
knowledge_points.practice: Decide whether each handler catches the error raised in its try; fix the wrong name.

knowledge_points.title: A variable assigned in a failed try does not exist afterwards
knowledge_points.worked_example:
try:
    n = int("x")
except ValueError:
    print("bad number")
print(n)
# bad number
# NameError: name 'n' is not defined
knowledge_points.practice: Find the line that raises NameError after a handled error; fix it by giving the variable a value in except or moving the use inside try.

topics.title: Several except clauses and reading the message with as
topics.summary: Handle different errors differently, group them in one handler, read the message with as e, and avoid catching everything.

knowledge_points.title: One except clause per kind of error
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output for a list of mixed values; add the missing handler.

knowledge_points.title: One handler for several errors: a tuple
knowledge_points.practice: Merge two identical handlers into one; predict which inputs reach it.

knowledge_points.title: except ... as e gives you the message
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the printed message for several failing conversions.

knowledge_points.title: Don't catch everything: a bare except hides real bugs
knowledge_points.worked_example:
try:
    totl = 1
    print(total)
except:
    print("something went wrong")
# something went wrong  (the NameError typo is hidden)
Name the errors you expect; a parent such as LookupError catches IndexError too.
knowledge_points.practice: Spot the handler that hides a typo and rewrite it to name the expected error.

topics.title: try ... else and finally
topics.summary: Use else for code that should run only when the try succeeded, and finally for code that must run either way, even after return.

knowledge_points.title: else runs only when nothing went wrong
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output for good and bad inputs; move a line from try into else.

knowledge_points.title: finally runs in every case
knowledge_points.worked_example:
finally:
        print("checked", s)
Added to to_int above: to_int("5") prints ok, checked 5; to_int("x") prints bad, checked x.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the order of try/except/else/finally blocks for three inputs; reorder the clauses into a valid statement.

knowledge_points.title: finally runs even when try returns
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def f():
    try:
        return "from try"
    finally:
        print("finally runs")

print(f())
# finally runs
# from try
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output order when try or except contains return.

topics.title: How an error travels up through function calls
topics.summary: Predict where an exception goes when a function does not catch it, choose the right level to catch it, and re-raise after reporting.

knowledge_points.title: An uncaught error leaves the function and goes to its caller
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which lines run after an error is raised two calls deep.

knowledge_points.title: The caller can catch an error raised inside a function
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output when the try is in the caller, in the helper, or missing.

knowledge_points.title: Catch where you can do something useful
knowledge_points.worked_example: parse_age can't know whether to re-ask, skip or quit, so it lets the error out; main(), which talks to the user, catches it and re-asks.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which function should hold the try/except in small programs.

knowledge_points.title: Report and re-raise with a bare raise
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output with and without the raise line.

topics.title: Skipping bad items in a loop
topics.summary: Put try/except inside a loop to skip or count values that fail, instead of stopping at the first bad one.

knowledge_points.title: try inside the loop skips just the bad item
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the total for lists with different bad values.

knowledge_points.title: try outside the loop stops at the first bad item
knowledge_points.practice: Compare inside vs outside placement; move the try to make the program skip instead of stop.

knowledge_points.title: Count the bad items as you go
knowledge_points.practice: Write a loop that sums the good values and counts the bad ones.

knowledge_points.title: Average only the good values, guarding against none
knowledge_points.practice: Write a function that averages the valid numbers in a list of strings and returns None when there are none.

topics.title: Raising an error from your own function
topics.summary: Use raise ValueError(...) to reject bad arguments with a clear message, and let the caller catch it.

knowledge_points.title: raise stops the function with an error
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output and errors for several calls; write the raise line for a given rule.

knowledge_points.title: The caller catches what you raise
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the printed message; write a caller that re-asks when set_volume raises.

knowledge_points.title: Raise instead of returning None for impossible input
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def safe_divide(a, b):
    if b == 0:
        return None
    return a / b

print(safe_divide(1, 0) + 1)
# TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'int'
The None travels on and fails far from the cause; raise ValueError("b must not be 0") fails at the cause.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose between raising and returning a value for described situations; rewrite a None-returning guard to raise.

knowledge_points.title: Pick a fitting built-in error type
knowledge_points.worked_example:
ValueError: right type, unacceptable value (age -3).
TypeError: wrong type altogether.
IndexError: a position out of range. Callers rely on the type to choose a handler.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the error type to raise for six described invalid inputs.

topics.title: Defining your own exception types
topics.summary: Define a one-line exception class, raise it, catch it by name, and base it on a built-in error so existing handlers still catch it.

knowledge_points.title: Define and raise your own exception
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the class line and raise statement for a described rule.

knowledge_points.title: Catch it by its name
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which handler runs when several custom and built-in handlers are listed.

knowledge_points.title: Base it on a built-in error so general handlers still work
knowledge_points.practice: Decide whether each handler catches a custom error given its base class.

topics.notes: Reconciliation: depends on classes.define_and_instantiate for the class statement; class X(Exception) is still read as a template until inheritance.define_subclass.

topics.title: Asking again until the user types a number
topics.summary: Write get_int(prompt): a while True loop with try/except ValueError that re-asks until int() succeeds, then add a range check.

knowledge_points.title: Loop until int() succeeds
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the prompts shown for a sequence of typed answers; reorder the lines (Parsons).

knowledge_points.title: Wrap it in a function: return ends the loop
knowledge_points.practice: Write get_float(prompt) by analogy; predict output for typed answers.

knowledge_points.title: Two kinds of bad input: not a number, and out of range
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the messages for x, 42, 7; fill in the range check.

knowledge_points.title: Bug: the risky line is outside the try
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix the misplaced conversion or the missing re-prompt in three variants.

topics.title: Guard conditions: check before you act
topics.summary: Protect risky operations (indexing, dividing) with guard conditions in the right order, and choose between checking first and trying first.

knowledge_points.title: The guardian pattern: check length before indexing
knowledge_points.worked_example:
line = ""
if len(line) > 0 and line[0] == "#":
    print("comment")
and stops at the first False, so line[0] is never evaluated for an empty line.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which lines run for empty and non-empty strings; add the missing guard.

knowledge_points.title: The guard must come first
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which of four conditions are safe for empty input; reorder the unsafe ones.

knowledge_points.title: Guard clauses at the top of a function
knowledge_points.practice: Write guard clauses for division, empty strings and negative sizes.

knowledge_points.title: Look before you leap vs try it and handle the error
knowledge_points.worked_example:
text = "-5"
print(text.isdigit())   # False, so an isdigit() check rejects a valid int
try: n = int(text) handles -5, " 7 " and "x" correctly.
Check first when the rule is simple; try when the check would repeat the conversion's own rules.
knowledge_points.practice: For given inputs, predict the result of an isdigit() check and of a try/int() version; choose the better style per case.

topics.title: Cleaning and validating text input
topics.summary: Normalise typed text with strip() and lower(), write an is_valid_...() check for its format, and re-ask until it passes.

knowledge_points.title: Clean before comparing
knowledge_points.worked_example:
answer = "  YES "
print(answer == "yes")                   # False
print(answer.strip().lower() == "yes")   # True
knowledge_points.practice: Predict comparisons with and without cleaning; add the cleaning step to a failing check.

knowledge_points.title: Write a validity check as a boolean function
knowledge_points.practice: Write is_valid_...() for a PIN, a username and a yes/no answer; predict results for edge inputs.

knowledge_points.title: Re-ask until the check passes
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of a validation loop; predict prompts for a sequence of typed answers.

knowledge_points.title: Know what your check accepts: test the edge inputs
knowledge_points.worked_example:
"-5".isdigit() and "3.5".isdigit() are both False; "" fails len checks; " 7" needs strip().
List the inputs a user might really type and run each through the check.
knowledge_points.practice: For a given validator, choose which inputs are wrongly accepted or rejected and fix it.

topics.title: Checking assumptions with assert
topics.summary: Write assert condition, message to stop the program when something you believe must be true is not, and know why assert is not for user input.

knowledge_points.title: assert does nothing when true, raises AssertionError when false
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 5
assert x > 0
print("passed")
assert 2 + 2 == 5
# passed
# AssertionError
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether each assert passes or raises.

knowledge_points.title: Add a message that shows the bad value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
assert x > 10, f"x is too small: {x}"
# AssertionError: x is too small: 5
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the AssertionError text; write an assert with a message for a stated rule.

knowledge_points.title: Assert your own assumptions, not the user's input
knowledge_points.worked_example:
assert total >= 0   # fine: a bug if this fails
python -O skips every assert:
assert 1 == 2, "never checked"  runs silently under -O.
Use if + raise (or a re-ask loop) for input from users.
knowledge_points.practice: For each situation, choose assert or input validation.

knowledge_points.title: Bug: parentheses turn an assert into an always-true tuple
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = -1
assert (x > 0, "x must be positive")
print("no error!")
# SyntaxWarning: assertion is always true, perhaps remove parentheses?
# no error!
knowledge_points.practice: Find the assert that can never fail and fix it.

topics.title: Writing a test function with assert
topics.summary: Write test_...() functions whose asserts check a function's return values, run them, and read which case failed.

knowledge_points.title: A test function: call, compare, assert
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def square(n):
    return n * n

def test_square():
    assert square(3) == 9
    assert square(-2) == 4
    assert square(0) == 0

test_square()
print("all tests passed")
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in expected values in asserts; write a three-assert test for a given function.

knowledge_points.title: A failing test points at the broken case
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which assert fails for a buggy implementation; explain why a single test case can pass by luck.

knowledge_points.title: Tests live beside the program, not inside main()
knowledge_points.worked_example: main() runs the program; test_square() checks it. Call the tests while developing, and keep main() free of asserts so users never see test failures.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder a file into helpers, tests and main (Parsons); choose which call runs the tests.

knowledge_points.title: Compare floats with a tolerance
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def average(a, b):
    return (a + b) / 2
print(average(0.1, 0.2) == 0.15)   # False (0.15000000000000002)
assert abs(average(0.1, 0.2) - 0.15) < 1e-9   # passes
knowledge_points.practice: Fix float asserts that fail by rounding error; predict which pass.

topics.title: Choosing test cases: typical, boundary and edge
topics.summary: Pick test inputs that find bugs: typical values with hand-worked answers, values at each boundary, edge cases like zero and empty, and one per branch.

knowledge_points.title: Work out the expected value by hand, not by running the code
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Expected values come from the spec: square(3) must be 9.
Copying whatever the code prints into the assert just records the bug.
knowledge_points.practice: Supply expected values for a function from its description; spot a test that was copied from buggy output.

knowledge_points.title: Test at the boundaries
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def grade(score):
    if score >= 90:
        return "A"
    elif score > 75:   # spec: 75 and up is B
        return "B"
    return "C"

assert grade(80) == "B"   # passes
assert grade(75) == "B"   # AssertionError: the boundary finds the bug
knowledge_points.practice: List the boundary values for given rules; choose the test that exposes an off-by-one.

knowledge_points.title: Edge cases: zero, negative, empty, one item
knowledge_points.worked_example: For count_vowels(text) test "", "a", "xyz", "AEIOU" as well as a normal sentence.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the edge cases for four function descriptions; write asserts for them.

knowledge_points.title: Cover every branch
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grade has three return lines, so at least three tests: one A, one B, one C.
A branch no test reaches can hide any bug.
knowledge_points.practice: Given a function with several branches, choose a minimal test set that reaches each branch.

topics.title: Writing functions you can test
topics.summary: Make code testable by returning results instead of printing them and taking values as parameters instead of calling input(); add a regression test for every bug fixed.

knowledge_points.title: A function that prints cannot be tested with ==
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}")

assert greet("Ada") == "Hello, Ada"
# Hello, Ada
# AssertionError   (greet returned None)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of asserting on printing functions.

knowledge_points.title: Return the result; let main() print it
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def greeting(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}"

assert greeting("Ada") == "Hello, Ada"
print(greeting("Ada"))   # Hello, Ada
knowledge_points.practice: Refactor a printing function to return, and write its test.

knowledge_points.title: Take values as parameters instead of calling input() inside
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which version of a function can be tested automatically; move the input() call to main().

knowledge_points.title: Regression test: every bug fixed gets a test
knowledge_points.worked_example: After fixing largest() for negative lists, add assert largest([-5, -2, -9]) == -2 so the bug can never return unnoticed.
knowledge_points.practice: Given a bug report and fix, write the regression assert.

topics.title: Testing that bad input raises an error
topics.summary: Write a test that passes only if a function raises the expected exception for invalid input.

knowledge_points.title: try the bad call; reaching the end means it did not raise
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of a raises-test (Parsons); predict whether it passes for a correct and a buggy function.

knowledge_points.title: A missing raise makes the test fail
knowledge_points.worked_example: If set_volume forgets its range check, set_volume(11) returns 11 and the test ends with AssertionError: expected ValueError.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which tests fail for three buggy versions of a validating function.

knowledge_points.title: Test both sides of the rule
knowledge_points.worked_example:
assert set_volume(10) == 10   # the boundary is allowed
plus a raises-test for 11 and one for -1.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the full test set (valid boundary, invalid on each side) for a validating function.

topics.title: Examples in docstrings as tests: doctest
topics.summary: Put REPL-style examples in a docstring and run them as tests with python -m doctest.

knowledge_points.title: Write examples as >>> lines and their results
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def square(n):
    """Return n squared.

    >>> square(3)
    9
    """
    return n * n
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the expected result lines of a docstring example.

knowledge_points.title: Run them: silence means they passed
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python -m doctest calc.py
(no output when every example passes)
If square returned n + n: Failed example: square(3) / Expected: 9 / Got: 6
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the doctest report for a buggy function.

knowledge_points.title: Expected output must match exactly
knowledge_points.worked_example:
>>> greeting("Ada")
'Hello, Ada'
A returned string is shown with quotes, as the REPL shows it; writing Hello, Ada without quotes fails.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix docstring examples whose expected lines would not match.

topics.title: The unittest module: TestCase and assert methods
topics.summary: Write tests as methods of a unittest.TestCase class using assertEqual, assertRaises and friends, and read unittest's report.

knowledge_points.title: A TestCase class with test_ methods
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the template for a new function; predict how many tests run.

knowledge_points.title: assertRaises for expected errors
knowledge_points.practice: Convert a try/except raises-test into assertRaises.

knowledge_points.title: Choosing assert methods: assertTrue, assertIn, assertAlmostEqual
knowledge_points.worked_example:
self.assertTrue(is_even(4))
self.assertIn("a", "cat")
self.assertAlmostEqual(average(0.1, 0.2), 0.15)   # tolerance built in
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the assert method for each check; fix a float test that uses assertEqual.

knowledge_points.title: Reading the report: dots, F and E
knowledge_points.worked_example:
..F
FAIL: test_zero ... AssertionError: 1 != 0
Ran 3 tests ... FAILED (failures=1)
. = pass, F = an assert failed, E = the test itself crashed.
knowledge_points.practice: Interpret reports: how many passed, which failed, and whether it was a failure or an error.

topics.title: Testing with pytest
topics.summary: Put test_ functions in a test_*.py file that imports the code under test, run pytest, and read its pass/fail report.

knowledge_points.title: A test file: import the function, write test_ functions
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# test_calc.py
from calc import square

def test_positive():
    assert square(2) == 4
    assert square(3) == 9

def test_zero():
    assert square(0) == 0
No calls at the bottom: pytest finds and runs every test_ function.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the import line and test names; choose which files and functions pytest will collect.

knowledge_points.title: Run pytest and read the summary
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ pip install pytest      (once)
$ pytest test_calc.py
..        [100%]
2 passed
Each dot is a passing test.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the summary line for a file with given passing and failing tests.

knowledge_points.title: Read a failure: pytest shows the values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
With square returning n + n:
F.
>       assert square(3) == 9
E       assert 6 == 9
E        +  where 6 = square(3)
FAILED test_calc.py::test_positive - assert 6 == 9
knowledge_points.practice: From a failure report, name the failing test, the call and the actual value; fix the function.

knowledge_points.title: Split cases into separate tests to see every failure
knowledge_points.worked_example: In one test, the first failing assert stops that test; test_zero still ran and passed. Several small tests show which cases break at once.
knowledge_points.practice: Split a long test function into focused tests with descriptive names.

topics.title: pytest.raises, parametrize and organising tests
topics.summary: Test expected exceptions with pytest.raises, run one test over many cases with @pytest.mark.parametrize, and organise test files in a tests folder that pytest discovers.

knowledge_points.title: with pytest.raises(...) checks that an error happens
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import pytest
from vol import set_volume

def test_too_loud():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        set_volume(11)
The test passes only if the indented call raises ValueError.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a try/except raises-test using pytest.raises; fill in the expected error type.

knowledge_points.title: DID NOT RAISE: the error you expected never happened
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def test_ok():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        set_volume(5)
# FAILED test_vol.py::test_ok - Failed: DID NOT RAISE <class 'ValueError'>
knowledge_points.practice: Predict pass/fail for raises-tests against correct and buggy functions.

knowledge_points.title: A tests folder and running everything with plain pytest
knowledge_points.worked_example:
project/
  calc.py
  tests/
    __init__.py
    test_calc.py
$ pytest      # finds every test_*.py file and test_ function
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which files and functions pytest collects from a folder listing.

knowledge_points.title: One test, many cases: @pytest.mark.parametrize
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import pytest
from calc import square

@pytest.mark.parametrize("n, expected", [(2, 4), (3, 9), (-1, 1)])
def test_square(n, expected):
    assert square(n) == expected
# $ pytest  ->  3 passed: one test per tuple
Each tuple fills n and expected for a separate test; a failing case is reported with its values, e.g. test_square[3-9].
knowledge_points.practice: Turn three near-identical test functions into one parametrized test; predict how many tests pytest reports.

topics.notes: Reconciliation: KP4 (parametrize) added because B09 left it to a stitching pass; pytest is not installed, so it was written from the pytest documentation and not run.

topics.title: Checking type hints with mypy
topics.summary: Run mypy on a file, read its errors, and fix the mismatches it finds before the code runs, including forgotten None cases.

knowledge_points.title: Run mypy and read the result
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ pip install mypy      (once)
$ mypy shapes.py
Success: no issues found in 1 source file
mypy reads the hints without running the program.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether mypy reports issues for small annotated files.

knowledge_points.title: Argument and return mismatches
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def half(n: int) -> int:
    return n / 2
print(double("ab"))
# error: Incompatible return value type (got "float", expected "int")  [return-value]
# error: Argument 1 to "double" has incompatible type "str"; expected "int"  [arg-type]
knowledge_points.practice: Given mypy errors, find the line and fix either the code or the hint.

knowledge_points.title: mypy catches the forgotten None case
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def find(names: list[str], target: str) -> int | None: ...
print(find(["a"], "a") + 1)
# error: Unsupported operand types for + ("None" and "int")  [operator]
Fix: check result is not None before using it.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code flagged for using a possibly-None value.

knowledge_points.title: Functions without hints are not checked
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def double(n):
    return n * 2
print(double("ab") + 1)
# mypy: Success: no issues found  (but it crashes when run)
Add hints to the functions you want checked.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict mypy's verdict for annotated vs unannotated versions of the same bug.
